titleText.es: [Poco después, en una confitería cercana] ::CRAC:: ::RUNRUN:: ::VRRRRRRR:: «No lo sé, agente. Tan sólo cogió un estante entero de pasteles de una paletada y salió huyendo».
titleText.en: [Shortly thereafter, at a nearby bakery] ::CRASH:: ::RUMBLE:: ::VRRRRRR:: '... I don't know, officer.  It just scooped up an entire rack of scones and drove away!'
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive and official xkcd source both identify comic #677. The English title text is copied verbatim from official xkcd; its two spaces after officer. are intentional. The raster joins the printed line-break fragments MIEN-/TRAS and POR-/QUE as MIENTRAS and PORQUE, treats RUNRUN as lexical Spanish onomatopoeia, inventories 4X4 as a nonlexical alphanumeric vehicle label, and inventories the silent ellipsis and final musical-note glyphs as nonlexical symbols.

regions.labelEs: MIRA ESE GILIPOLLAS EN SU 4X4, CREYÉNDOSE MUY MALO POR CHUPAR GASOLINA MIENTRAS CONDUCE POR LOS SUBURBIOS.

excludedUnits.rationale: This alphanumeric vehicle classification is visible source text but not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Mira is the positive informal singular command of mirar, used here to direct one familiar listener's attention.
Creyéndose adds a belief held at the same time as the observed action; there is no separate form of estar before it.
Se attaches to creyendo as part of creerse, and the written accent preserves the original stress.
Creyéndose supplies the self-directed belief, and muy malo supplies the intensified masculine singular description.
Por introduces the reason, while chupar stays in its unchanged -ar dictionary form.
Por marks the area followed as a driving route; natural English can describe movement around or through that area.
Que opens the hoped-for negative alternative, while the rest of the idea is left unstated because the preceding question makes it clear.

regions.labelEs: MIRA ESE GILIPOLLAS PAGADO DE SÍ MISMO, CREYÉNDOSE MEJOR QUE NOSOTROS PORQUE CONDUCE UN HÍBRIDO.

applications.explanationEn: Mira is again the positive informal singular command used to direct one familiar listener's attention.
Pagado and mismo use masculine singular endings for the man being described, while de sí links the description back to that same person.
Creyéndose adds a simultaneous belief without a separate form of estar.
Se attaches to creyendo as part of creerse, and the written accent preserves the original stress.
Creyéndose supplies the self-directed belief, while mejor que nosotros supplies the complete comparative description.
Mejor supplies the irregular comparison, que introduces its other side, and nosotros supplies the group used as the comparison point.

excludedUnits.rationale: The three dots form a silent reaction mark rather than a Spanish lexical word.
These three musical-note glyphs indicate whistling and are symbols rather than Spanish words.

cards.answerEn: look; listen; hey (to get someone's attention)
cards.noteEn: Mira is the positive command form of mirar used with one familiar person. At the start of a comment, it often simply gets the listener's attention, like “look,” “listen,” or “hey,” without asking them to look at an object.

example.en: Listen, I have an idea.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

example.en: Open the window.

cards.noteEn: Ese points to a masculine singular noun that is not presented as right next to the speaker. Feminine singular is esa.

example.en: I do not recognize that sound.

cards.noteEn: Gilipollas is a strong informal insult widely associated with Spain. It can keep the same form for a man or a woman.

example.en: Don't be a jerk.

cards.questionEn: Why does changing from the 4x4 to a hybrid fail to satisfy the observers?
cards.answerEn: They first condemn fuel waste, then reinterpret the environmentally friendlier choice as smugness, creating a no-win judgment; the driver responds with absurd construction machinery.
cards.noteEn: The joke turns shifting social criticism into escalation. The driver's attempt to avoid one label produces the opposite criticism, and the low RUNRUN announces an outsized backhoe retaliation. The official title text extends that absurd rampage into a nearby bakery.
Su agrees with the possessed thing, not with the owner. The same Spanish form can mean his, her, its, their, or formal your; the surrounding context identifies the owner.

example.en: Carlos opens his laptop.

cards.answerEn: thinking of himself as; considering himself
cards.noteEn: Creyéndose comes from the pronominal verb creerse. Creyendo is creer in its -iendo action form, and se is attached for the person being described. A description normally follows.

example.en: Luis left thinking himself invincible.

cards.promptEs: -ando / -iendo para una acción simultánea o un medio
cards.questionEn: How can you add an action that happens at the same time or explains how something is done?
cards.answerEn: Use the action form ending in -ando or -iendo, such as hablando or corriendo.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls this form the gerund. It does not change for the person. Used on its own, it can describe a simultaneous action or the means used: Entró corriendo means the person entered by running. This differs from estar plus the same form, which focuses on an action in progress.

example.en: She came in running.

cards.questionEn: How do you attach the matching marker of a pronominal verb to an ongoing-action form?
cards.answerEn: Join me, te, se, nos, os, or se to the end of the -ando or -iendo form, adding a written accent when needed to preserve the original stress.
cards.noteEn: A pronominal verb is learned with se, such as verse or prepararse. Its short marker changes with the person. When the marker follows an ongoing-action form as one word, spelling may need an accent: viendo + me becomes viéndome, and preparando + se becomes preparándose.

example.en: I am getting ready to leave.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone thinks of themself as having a certain quality?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of creerse followed by the description.
cards.noteEn: Creerse is a pronominal verb, meaning that it uses a short marker matching the person: me creo, te crees, se cree, nos creemos, os creéis, or se creen. The description can be an adjective or comparison and changes to match the person when its form allows. With the -iendo action form, the marker can attach: creyendo plus se becomes creyéndose.

example.en: Raúl thinks he is indispensable.

cards.noteEn: Malo ordinarily means bad. In an informal boast or judgment about a person, especially after creerse, it can sarcastically suggest being tough, dangerous, or intimidating.

example.es: Se cree muy malo delante de sus amigos.
example.en: He thinks he is very tough in front of his friends.

cards.promptEs: por + verbo en forma de diccionario (motivo)
cards.questionEn: How do you give an action as the reason something happens?
cards.answerEn: Use por, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, such as llegar, perder, or salir. A small attached word may remain on that form, as in por quejarme. Por presents the action as the cause or reason; para plus the same kind of verb normally presents an intended purpose instead.

example.es: Llegó tarde por perder el autobús.
example.en: He arrived late because he missed the bus.

cards.noteEn: Chupar literally means to suck. With fuel, electricity, or another resource, informal Spanish can use it for consuming a large amount.

example.en: That engine guzzles a lot of gasoline.

cards.noteEn: Conduce is the present form of conducir for he, she, or formal singular you.

example.en: Ana drives to work.

cards.answerEn: through; along; down; via (a movement path)
cards.noteEn: Por can mark the path followed during movement. English may choose through, along, down, or via according to the route.

example.en: We went down the path.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: smug; self-satisfied (in pagado de sí mismo)
cards.noteEn: Pagado can literally mean paid, but pagado de sí mismo is a fixed description of a man who is excessively pleased with himself.

example.en: He seemed full of himself.

cards.questionEn: How do you describe someone as smug or excessively pleased with themself?
cards.answerEn: Use pagado de sí mismo for a man or pagada de sí misma for a woman.
cards.noteEn: This is a fixed, critical description meaning self-satisfied or full of oneself. The endings match the person: pagados de sí mismos for a masculine or mixed plural group and pagadas de sí mismas for a feminine plural group.

example.es: Parecía muy pagada de sí misma.
example.en: She seemed very full of herself.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links pagado to sí mismo
cards.noteEn: De is required inside the fixed description pagado de sí mismo. Translate the expression as a unit rather than assigning de its ordinary meaning of of or from.

example.es: Está muy pagada de sí misma.
example.en: She is very full of herself.

cards.answerEn: himself; herself; itself; themselves (after a preposition)
cards.noteEn: After a preposition such as de, para, or por, stressed sí points back to a third-person subject. It has a written accent and often appears with mismo, misma, mismos, or mismas for emphasis.

example.es: Guardó el secreto para sí misma.
example.en: She kept the secret to herself.

cards.noteEn: After a form such as mí, ti, or sí, mismo emphasizes that very person. Its ending changes to match: misma, mismos, or mismas.

example.en: Believe in yourself.

cards.noteEn: Mejor compares one option with another. It does not change for gender: una solución mejor and un plan mejor both use mejor.

example.en: We need a better idea.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone does something better than someone else?
cards.answerEn: Use mejor for “better,” then que before the person or thing being compared.
cards.noteEn: Mejor already contains the idea of “more good” or “better,” so do not add más before it. When mejor describes how an action is done, it does not change for gender or number. Que introduces the other side of the comparison.

example.en: Ana cooks better than I do.

cards.noteEn: Used as a masculine noun after un, híbrido can stand for an understood vehículo or coche híbrido.

example.en: They bought a small hybrid car.

cards.noteEn: Runrún is Spanish onomatopoeia for a repeated low mechanical sound or murmur. Comics may print it without the written accent and in capitals as RUNRUN.

example.es: Se oía el runrún del motor.
example.en: The engine's low rumble could be heard.
